summary: Defines a common YANG module meant to be reused by various VPN-related modules, such as those for Layer 3 and Layer 2 VPN network models. It holds shared definitions so the other models stay consistent.

eli5.summary: A shared box of building blocks used by many VPN models.

subtitle: One shared YANG module of identities, types and groupings that every Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN model can reuse.

tldr.problem: The YANG models for VPN services (L3SM, L2SM, L3NM, L2NM) all contain many of the same data nodes and structures, and copying them from one model into another made one model look as if it depended on another.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9181 defines a single module, ietf-vpn-common, holding reusable identities, types and groupings (VPN description, status, route targets, route distinguishers, ports, QoS classification and more) that any VPN module can import.
tldr.outcome: The module is used by the L3NM in RFC 9182 and is meant for the L2NM and for future revisions of the L3SM and L2SM. It defines no writable data nodes of its own.

today: RFC 9181 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the common module that the L3NM in RFC 9182 builds on.

sections.title: Why a Common VPN Module
sections.content:
The IETF already had YANG modules for VPN services, such as the Layer 3 VPN Service Model (L3SM, RFC 8299) and the Layer 2 VPN Service Model (L2SM, RFC 8466). The Layer 3 VPN Network Model (L3NM, RFC 9182) and the Layer 2 VPN Network Model (L2NM) were also in the works. Many data nodes and structures appear in all of these models, or in at least some of them.

RFC 9181 defines one module, ietf-vpn-common, with a set of identities, types and groupings that other VPN modules can reuse. The reuse is meant to work independently of the layer (Layer 2 or Layer 3) and of the type of module (network model or service model), including future revisions of the L3SM and L2SM.
sections.eli5: Several VPN recipes all used the same ingredients. So the authors put those ingredients in one shared pantry that every recipe can borrow from.

sections.title: Features and Identities
sections.content:
The module defines a set of common VPN-related features. They cover encapsulations (dot1Q, QinQ, link aggregation and VXLAN), multicast, and routing (BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection and VRRP).

It also defines identities, which are named labels that other modules can point to. Two examples the RFC highlights are service-type, which says what kind of VPN service this is, and vpn-signaling-type, which says how the service is signaled.

  • Service types include L3VPN, VPLS using BGP, VPLS using LDP, VPWS, BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPN, EVPN and PBB-EVPN.
  • Signaling types include L2VPNs using BGP, LDP and L2TP.

The module covers both IPv4 and IPv6 identities, plus multicast identities for IGMPv1, IGMPv2, IGMPv3, MLDv1, MLDv2 and PIM. The full list also covers address families, VPN topologies, network access types, operational and administrative status, site or node role, VPN service constraints, routing protocols, route import and export policies, bandwidth and QoS.
sections.eli5: Identities are like name tags. Instead of every model inventing its own words for kinds of VPN, they all pick a tag from the same table.

sections.title: The Reusable Groupings
sections.content:
A YANG grouping is a block of data nodes that another module can pull in with uses. The common module provides these:

  • vpn-description: an identifier, a name, a textual description and a customer name.
  • vpn-profile-cfg: valid provider-defined profiles (encryption, QoS, BFD, forwarding, routing and external connectivity) that can be bound to a VPN. The RFC makes no assumption about what is inside such profiles.
  • oper-status-timestamp and service-status: administrative and operational status with a last-change time, usable for a whole service or an endpoint.
  • underlay-transport: either an abstract transport instance (for example a VPN+ instance identifier, a virtual network identifier or a network slice name) or an ordered list of the actual protocols to enable.
  • vpn-route-targets and route-distinguisher: Route Target and Route Distinguisher handling for BGP-enabled VPNs.
  • vpn-components-group and placement-constraints: grouping VPN nodes, accesses or sites so that, for example, diversity or redundancy constraints can be applied per group.
  • ports: ranges of source and destination port numbers, plus operators.
  • qos-classification-policy: QoS classification rules based on Layer 3/4 and application match criteria.

The QoS match criteria reuse groupings from the packet fields module in RFC 8519. Any Layer 4 protocol can be named under protocol, but only TCP and UDP specific match criteria are elaborated in this version. The module does not support matching on the payload of transport protocols that run over TCP or UDP; the RFC leaves that to future revisions.
sections.eli5: A grouping is a ready-made form with some boxes already printed on it, like a name box and a status box. Any VPN model can photocopy the form instead of drawing the boxes again.

sections.title: Route Distinguishers and Route Targets
sections.content:
Two groupings deal with BGP VPN plumbing. vpn-route-targets models Route Target import and export rules and works for both L3VPNs (RFC 4364) and L2VPNs. It is modeled as a list so that other modules can reuse it wherever an RT identifier is needed.

The route-distinguisher grouping supports four assignment modes: direct assignment, full automatic assignment, automatic assignment from a given pool, and no assignment. It also handles deployments where only the Assigned Number subfield of the RD is assigned from a pool, while the Administrator subfield is set to something such as the Router ID of the VPN node. That subfield can be assigned explicitly, automatically from a pool, or fully automatically.
sections.eli5: Route distinguishers are like unique stickers that keep two customers' identical house numbers from being mixed up. The module lets you pick a sticker yourself, have one handed out automatically, or use none.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. The RFC restates that the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and points to the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) for restricting what users can do.

By itself the module exposes no writable data nodes, no read-only state and no RPCs, so it adds no security issues of its own. Modules that use these groupings must work out their own security considerations. The RFC gives one example: reusing some groupings exposes privacy-related information such as customer-name, and disclosing it may violate the customer-provider trust relationship.
sections.eli5: The shared parts are only blueprints, so there is nothing to break into. The models that actually use them have to lock their own doors.

sections.title: Why Not Just Copy Between Models
sections.content:
Appendix A explains the design choice. Early versions of the L3NM reused many data nodes defined in the L3SM. That approach was dropped because it looked as if deploying the L3NM depends on the L3SM, which is not required: a provider may use the L3NM to build L3VPN services without ever exposing the L3SM to customers.

Early versions of the L2NM likewise reused nodes from the L2SM and the L3NM, for example by importing the L3NM module and using its service-status grouping. That too was read as the L2NM requiring support for the L3NM. A neutral common module removes the apparent dependency.
sections.eli5: If two toys borrowed parts from each other, it looked like you needed to buy both. A separate shared parts box means you can buy just the toy you want.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-vpn-common in the IETF XML Registry. It also registered the YANG module ietf-vpn-common in the YANG Module Names registry, with prefix vpn-common and this RFC as the reference. The module is not maintained by IANA.
sections.eli5: The module was given its official name in a public list, so nobody else can use the same name for something different.
